speaker: Mark Chen
title: How OpenAI Shapes Its Research And What's Next - EP 46 Mark Chen
question: When rival AI labs pull ahead on public benchmarks, why is reacting with incremental updates a losing research strategy?
guest: The AI research landscape today is much more competitive than it's ever been, and the important thing is not to get caught up in that competitive dynamic. You can always ship an incremental update that puts you in front of a competitor for a couple weeks or a couple months. I don't think that's the long-term sustainable way to do research, because if you crack the next paradigm, that matters so much more. You shape the evolution of it, and you understand all the side research directions around that sphere of ideas. Look at our RL program as an example: we bet more than two years ago that we'd crack RL on language models, which was a very unpopular bet at the time. Back then the environment was, 'There's a pre-training machine working great and a post-training machine working great—why invest in something else?' Today everyone agrees thinking in language models is a primitive you can't live without. So we're really there to make bold bets and build algorithms that scale to orders of magnitude more compute.

points.core: Incremental benchmark updates only secure a fleeting competitive lead for brief periods.
points.note: Accept: short-lived leads of weeks or months, temporary leaderboard jumps that rivals quickly erase. Do not credit: generic claims that incremental work is unambitious without noting how quickly the lead evaporates.

points.core: Cracking a new paradigm lets a lab map the adjacent research frontier.
points.note: Accept: shaping a new paradigm's evolution, discovering surrounding side research directions, or owning the broader idea tree before competitors. Do not credit: vague slogans about innovation or first-mover advantage without mentioning downstream research directions.

points.core: Transformative paradigm bets look unpopular early because existing training pipelines already work.
points.note: Accept: internal skepticism toward unproven bets like early RL on LLMs when current pre-training or post-training machines are already delivering strong returns. Do not credit: generic claims that big bets are risky or hard to fund.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Reacting with incremental updates is a losing strategy because it lets competitors set your research agenda while guaranteeing you stay behind them.

Public benchmarks are lagging indicators: a rival's lead reflects bets they made a year or more ago. If you respond by shipping small tweaks to close the gap, you are chasing where they were, not where they are going; by the time you catch up, they have moved on. You also inherit their choice of what matters, optimizing for metrics they picked and are already best positioned to win.

Incrementalism has compounding costs too. It diverts scarce compute and top researchers from long-horizon bets to short-cycle patching, and it encourages benchmark overfitting, where scores rise without real capability gains. It also erodes the exploratory culture that produces step changes. Major advances in AI, such as transformers, large-scale pretraining and reasoning models, came from sustained work on different approaches, not from marginal tuning of the incumbent method.

The better response is to treat a rival's lead as information: understand what drove it, then invest in the bets that could leapfrog them rather than match them.

points.why: The response argues that incremental updates chase a moving target but never says that any benchmark lead they secure quickly disappears.
The response advocates bets that could leapfrog rivals but does not explain how cracking a new paradigm reveals adjacent research directions.
The response mentions incumbent methods but never links their success to early skepticism about transformative bets.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Reacting to a rival’s benchmark lead with incremental updates mistakes a lagging indicator for the true frontier. Major capability leaps reflect foundational bets—such as new architectures, data paradigms, or training regimes—initiated months or years earlier. Scrambling to close that gap with minor patches traps a lab near its current local maximum while competitors are already compounding their next generational shift.

Chasing public leaderboards also triggers Goodhart’s law. Short-term sprints incentivize narrow optimizations, like targeted post-training or benchmark-specific tuning, that inflate scores on saturating, contamination-prone evaluations without advancing general reasoning or real-world utility.

Most importantly, reactive release cycles fragment scarce compute and attention. Diverting clusters and top researchers toward defensive point updates starves the high-variance, long-horizon experiments needed to bend the capability curve. Labs that play catch-up on public metrics surrender their own research roadmap, trading breakthrough discovery for fleeting parity on a rapidly depreciating scoreboard.

points.why: The candidate describes briefly matching rivals’ scores but never claims that incremental updates can put a lab ahead and that the lead quickly disappears.
The candidate links foundational bets to capability gains but does not explain how a breakthrough reveals adjacent research directions.
The candidate describes long-horizon experiments as uncertain and resource-intensive but does not connect early skepticism to the success of existing training pipelines.

noweb.answer: Reacting to rival breakthroughs with incremental updates traps an AI lab in a perpetual game of catch-up. Because public releases reflect research completed months earlier, optimizing for a competitor's current benchmark scores means aiming at a target rivals have already moved past. Worse, incrementalism carries a steep opportunity cost: finite compute, researcher attention, and engineering bandwidth spent on short-term tuning, data patching, and frequent release cycles are diverted away from the long-horizon architectural, algorithmic, and scaling bets required to produce step-function leaps. Chasing leaderboards also invites Goodhart's law, tempting teams to overfit to narrow, saturating evaluations rather than building generalizable capabilities that compound over time. By trading foundational exploration for temporary parity, a lab fragments its roadmap around competitors' priorities and hits diminishing returns on an aging paradigm just as rivals ship the next major advance.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Chasing a rival's benchmark lead with incremental updates usually fails for a few connected reasons.

First, you're aiming at where the rival used to be. A published score reflects work they finished months earlier. By the time your tuned model catches up, they've moved on, so you stay a cycle behind.

Second, Goodhart's law applies: a benchmark that becomes the goal stops measuring much. Teams tuning for a leaderboard tend to overfit, absorb test data into training, and gain points that don't show up in real-world use. Many benchmarks also saturate fast, so small gains carry less and less meaning.

Third, the big jumps have come from changes in approach, not small refinements. Scaling laws, RLHF and reasoning models trained with reinforcement learning to think longer each reset the field. Reactive tuning pulls compute and talent away from the long-shot bets that produce those jumps.

That said, it isn't always a losing strategy. Fast followers like DeepSeek have shown that efficient copying and steady engineering can close gaps cheaply. The real weakness is having no research direction of your own, not making incremental progress as such.

noweb.answer:
Reacting to a rival’s benchmark lead with incremental updates traps a lab in a permanent game of catch-up. Public benchmarks are lagging indicators that quickly saturate and reward narrow optimization over genuine capability. When a lab diverts top researchers and scarce compute into minor tuning cycles just to reclaim leaderboard spots, it pays a steep opportunity cost: those resources are pulled away from the high-risk, foundational work—new architectures, training paradigms, or data breakthroughs—that produces actual step-change progress.

Worse, chasing yesterday’s scores invites Goodhart’s Law, encouraging overfitting to static tests at the expense of real-world generalization and long-term scientific depth. Because training and shipping even small updates takes months, an incremental response typically lands just as competitors unveil their next major leap, leaving the reactive lab perpetually a generation behind. Durable leadership in AI comes from defining the next frontier rather than polishing responses to the last one.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
By the time a rival posts a higher benchmark score, it has already done the research behind that result and may have moved on. If you redirect your team toward closing the public gap, you’re spending your next research cycle chasing their last one.

Small updates can improve a score and buy time, but a leaderboard rarely tells you which training choices drove the gain or which capability will matter next. If each release resets your priorities, longer experiments get interrupted and your team has less time to develop ideas that could give it a durable lead.

Use rival results to test your assumptions, then protect time for research into the bottlenecks your own evaluations reveal. Incremental experiments are valuable when they answer a question that matters to that research agenda.

A rival’s benchmark lead tells you what it has already achieved, not what it’s working on now. If you spend your next research cycle closing that gap, you may reach parity just as the rival makes its next advance. Worse, a higher score can reward a narrow fix even when the underlying limitation persists.

Incremental updates are valuable when they test a hypothesis or solve a problem users face. They become a losing strategy when the leaderboard sets the research agenda. You give up time for riskier experiments that could produce a capability no rival has yet demonstrated.
